title: What are the two categories of RDD/DataFrame operations — transformations (lazy: `filter`, `map`, `flatMap`, `groupByKey`, `join`, `select`, `sorted`, `distinct`) vs actions (eager, trigger execution: `collect`, `count`, `show`, `saveAsTextFile`, `write`) — and what is lazy evaluation?
shortTitle: Transformations vs actions and lazy evaluation

s1_definition.profdef: Spark operations fall into two categories. Transformations are lazy operations that take an RDD or DataFrame and return a new one, building up a logical plan without executing anything; examples include filter, map, flatMap, groupByKey, join, select, and distinct. Actions are eager operations that trigger execution of the accumulated plan and return a result to the Driver or write to storage; examples include collect, count, show, saveAsTextFile, and write. Lazy evaluation is the principle that transformations only record intent until an action forces the whole optimized plan to run.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a manager at the National Bank of India writing a to-do list for processing statements: "filter Rajesh's transactions, convert amounts to rupees, group by month." Writing each item on the list is a transformation — it costs nothing, the clerks are still sitting idle. Only when the manager says "now go and total it up and print the report" — that command is an action — do the clerks spring into motion and do all the listed steps at once. Because the manager wrote the full list before anyone moved, he could reorder and merge steps for efficiency instead of making the clerks run back and forth for each line.
s1_definition.oneliner: Transformations build a lazy plan and return a new dataset, actions execute the plan and return a result, and lazy evaluation lets Spark optimize the whole chain before running it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark operations fall into two categories. Transformations are lazy operations that take an RDD or DataFrame and return a new one, building up a logical plan without executing anything; examples include filter, map, flatMap, groupByKey, join, select, and distinct. Actions are eager operations that trigger execution of the accumulated plan and return a result to the Driver or write to storage; examples include collect, count, show, saveAsTextFile, and write. Lazy evaluation is the principle that transformations only record intent until an action forces the whole optimized plan to run.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a manager at the National Bank of India writing a to-do list for processing statements: "filter Rajesh's transactions, convert amounts to rupees, group by month." Writing each item on the list is a transformation — it costs nothing, the clerks are still sitting idle. Only when the manager says "now go and total it up and print the report" — that command is an action — do the clerks spring into motion and do all the listed steps at once. Because the manager wrote the full list before anyone moved, he could reorder and merge steps for efficiency instead of making the clerks run back and forth for each line.

**One line to remember:** Transformations build a lazy plan and return a new dataset, actions execute the plan and return a result, and lazy evaluation lets Spark optimize the whole chain before running it.

sections.s2_technical:
A transformation never runs on its own. When you call filter, map, flatMap, groupByKey, join, select, sorted, or distinct, Spark simply extends the lineage graph with a new node describing the operation and hands you back a new RDD or DataFrame. Nothing is read, nothing is computed, no executor does any work. This is why you can chain a dozen transformations instantly even on a dataset of billions of rows — you are only describing the computation, not performing it.

An action is what forces the whole thing to execute. When you call collect, count, show, saveAsTextFile, or write, Spark looks at the entire lineage leading up to that point, hands it to the Catalyst optimizer for DataFrames or the DAGScheduler for RDDs, builds stages and tasks, and runs them across the executors. An action either brings a result back to the Driver, like count returning a number or collect returning a list, or it writes output to storage, like write saving Parquet files. Each action triggers a fresh execution of the lineage, which is an important and often-missed point: if you call two actions on the same chain without caching, Spark recomputes the whole chain twice.

Lazy evaluation is the engine behind this split, and it exists for optimization. Because Spark sees the full chain before executing, the Catalyst optimizer can push a filter down so less data is read from disk, prune columns you never use, combine adjacent maps into a single pass, and reorder joins. If Spark executed every transformation eagerly, it would materialize huge intermediate datasets it does not need and lose all these opportunities. A quick way to distinguish the two in practice: if the return type is another RDD or DataFrame, it is a transformation; if the return type is a value, a collection in the Driver, or Unit from writing, it is an action.

There is a further distinction within transformations that matters for performance: narrow transformations like map and filter need no data movement because each output partition depends on one input partition, while wide transformations like groupByKey and join require a shuffle that moves data across the network. A senior nuance is that a stray action in a loop, or forgetting to cache before multiple actions, is one of the most common causes of slow Spark jobs, because each action re-triggers the entire lineage. In banking reporting I always counted my actions deliberately — one write at the end, not a count after every step.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The bank wants to describe a chain of cleaning steps cheaply, without running each one immediately. This is exactly what lazy transformations do — they just record intent.

Problem 2 — Eventually the report must actually be produced and the total returned. This is exactly what an action does — it triggers execution.

Problem 3 — Calling two reports on the same chain should not silently recompute everything twice unnoticed. This is exactly why understanding "each action re-runs the lineage" matters.

The mini-project models this with a `LazyDataset` that records transformations as a list of pending operations and only executes them inside action methods. Transformations filter, map, and distinct return new `LazyDataset` objects (and log that they are lazy). Actions count and collect run the recorded chain and log an execution counter so you can literally see that two actions trigger two executions. The demo processes Rajesh's and Priya's transactions.

# Run the transformations vs actions demo
java -cp target/transformations-actions-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.txa.TxaDemo

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions — Rajesh Rs.1000, Priya Rs.500, Rajesh Rs.3000.

Step 1: The base LazyDataset is created holding all three transactions. The plan list is empty. No work has happened.

Step 2: filter is called to keep only Rajesh's transactions. This records a step in the plan and returns a new dataset. The data is untouched and nothing executes — the log confirms it is lazy.

Step 3: map is called to extract amounts. This records a second step and returns another new dataset. We now have a two-step plan but zero executions.

Step 4: The first action, count, runs. It executes the plan once — applying filter then map to the base data — producing the amounts Rs.1000 and Rs.3000, then counting them as two. The execution counter shows execution number one.

Step 5: The second action, collect, runs on the same chain. Because nothing was cached, it executes the entire plan again from the base data, producing the same two amounts. The execution counter shows execution number two, proving each action re-triggers the lineage.

Step 6: The final collected result is the list of Rs.1000 and Rs.3000. The journey shows transformations costing nothing and actions driving every execution.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] transformation filter() recorded (LAZY — nothing runs)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] transformation map() recorded (LAZY — nothing runs)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Chain built. No execution happened yet.
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] ACTION triggers execution #1 of 2 recorded transformations
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] count() = 2
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] ACTION triggers execution #2 of 2 recorded transformations
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] collect() = [1000, 3000]
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Transformations vs Actions ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Builder/Fluent: chained transformations build a plan        │
  │     WHY: readable pipeline, defers execution                 │
  │  Command: each transformation is a recorded operation        │
  │     WHY: store, optimize, then run the whole command list    │
  │  Lazy Initialization: plan runs only when an action fires    │
  │     WHY: optimize the full DAG; avoid wasted work            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: LazyDataset only records + executes a plan               │
  │  O: new transformation = new method, execute() unchanged     │
  │  D: steps stored as Function abstraction, not concrete logic │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               LazyDataset<T>                 │
  │─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ - source: List<T>                            │
  │ - plan: List<Function<...>>   ◆ owns recipe  │
  │ - executionCounter: int (static)             │
  │─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ + filter(Predicate): LazyDataset<T>   (lazy) │
  │ + map(Function): LazyDataset<R>       (lazy) │
  │ + distinct(): LazyDataset<T>          (lazy) │
  │ + count(): long                       (ACTION)│
  │ + collect(): List<T>                  (ACTION)│
  │ - execute(): List<Object>                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Query Lifecycle ─────────────────────────────

  [PLANNING] ──transformation──→ [PLANNING] (plan grows)
       │
       │ action called
       ▼
  [EXECUTING] ──→ [RESULT RETURNED] ──(new action)──→ back to EXECUTING

  ── Call Chain ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. TxaDemo.main()
  2.   → filter(...)   → records step, returns new dataset (lazy)
  3.   → map(...)      → records step, returns new dataset (lazy)
  4.   → count()       → execute() #1 → 2
  5.   → collect()     → execute() #2 → [1000, 3000]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark operations come in two categories, and knowing the difference is fundamental to writing efficient jobs. Transformations are lazy: operations like filter, map, flatMap, groupByKey, join, select, and distinct take a dataset and return a new dataset, but they execute nothing — they just extend the logical plan. Actions are eager: operations like collect, count, show, saveAsTextFile, and write trigger execution of the accumulated plan and either return a result to the Driver or write output to storage. A simple rule I use is that if the return type is another DataFrame or RDD it is a transformation, and if it returns a value or writes data it is an action.

Lazy evaluation is the principle tying this together, and it exists purely for optimization. Because Spark does not run transformations immediately, it sees the entire chain before executing and can let the Catalyst optimizer push filters down to read less data, prune unused columns, fuse adjacent operations into one pass, and reorder joins. If every transformation ran eagerly, Spark would materialize huge intermediate results and lose all of those optimizations. The subtle and important consequence is that every action re-triggers the whole lineage, so calling several actions on the same uncached chain recomputes everything each time.

In my project at the National Bank of India this understanding directly shaped performance. I built long chains of transformations freely because they cost nothing, but I was deliberate about actions — ideally one write at the end of a report rather than a count or show after every step. When I genuinely needed multiple actions on the same intermediate result, I cached it first so Spark computed it once and reused it. That discipline of thinking in terms of lazy transformations and counted actions is what kept our nightly reporting jobs fast and predictable.

keyPoints: Parquet: columnar, compressed, schema — best for analytics
Avro: row-based, schema evolution, compact — best for Kafka
ORC: columnar, optimized for Hive — similar to Parquet
Choose: Parquet for reads (analytics), Avro for writes (streaming)
